breakfast.name: Alloco (Fried Plantains)
instructions: Slice plantains
Deep fry until golden
Serve with diced chili and onion
breakfast.description: Fried plantains with chili — Ivorian street food.

breakfast.name: Garba (Attieké with Tuna)
instructions: Fluff attiéké
Top with tuna, onion, tomato, chili
Season with oil and Maggi
breakfast.description: Cassava couscous with fried tuna — the Ivorian fast food.

breakfast.name: Garba (Attieke with Fried Tuna)
ingredients: Attiéké (fermented cassava couscous — Ivory Coast's staple)
instructions: Attiéké is Ivory Coast's unique contribution — fermented cassava processed into couscous-like grains
Fry tuna until crispy — canned tuna works and is the street version
Dice raw onion and tomato
Serve attiéké on a plate, fried tuna on top
Add raw onion, tomato, hot pepper
Drizzle oil, add Maggi seasoning
This is Abidjan's most popular street meal — named 'Garba' after Garba Town, a market area
Garba vendors are everywhere in Abidjan — it's the city's fuel
Cheap, filling, fast — the definition of Ivorian street food
breakfast.description: Ivory Coast's most eaten street food — fermented cassava couscous (attiéké) with fried tuna, raw onion, and hot pepper. Named after Garba Town in Abidjan. Attiéké is Ivory Coast's unique contribution to world starches — a fermented cassava product found nowhere else.

breakfast.name: Bouillie d'Igname (Yam Porridge)
instructions: Boil yam until very soft — 15-20 min
Mash or blend until smooth and creamy
Add milk, sugar, vanilla, cinnamon
The consistency should be thick and porridge-like
Serve warm — this is Ivorian comfort breakfast
Yam is one of West Africa's most important crops
The creamy, starchy, sweet porridge is deeply satisfying
Simple, nourishing, warm — morning perfection
breakfast.description: Ivorian yam porridge — white yam boiled and mashed into a creamy, sweet, spiced porridge with milk and cinnamon. Yam is one of West Africa's most important crops, and this porridge showcases its versatility beyond the usual boiled-and-pounded preparations.

lunch.name: Sauce Graine (Palm Nut Soup)
instructions: Extract cream from palm nut pulp
Brown meat, sauté vegetables
Add palm cream and water
Simmer 35 min
Serve with fufu or rice
lunch.description: Rich palm nut cream soup — a cornerstone of Ivorian cuisine.

lunch.name: Kédjenou (Slow-Cooked Chicken)
instructions: Put all ingredients in pot without water
Cover tightly
Cook over low heat 90 min, shaking occasionally
Chicken cooks in its own juices
lunch.description: Sealed-pot chicken — no added water, pure flavor.

lunch.name: Sauce Arachide (Peanut Sauce with Rice)
instructions: Brown meat in palm oil
Sauté onion, garlic, add tomato paste — fry until dark
Add peanut paste dissolved in warm water — stir until smooth
Add eggplant, Scotch bonnet
Simmer 30-40 min until meat is tender and sauce is thick
The peanut sauce should coat the back of a spoon — rich and creamy
Season with Maggi, salt
Serve over steamed rice — the peanut sauce on white rice is the visual
Sauce arachide is West Africa's universal peanut stew — Ivory Coast's version uses more palm oil
The deep orange color from palm oil mixed with brown peanut sauce is distinctive
lunch.description: Ivory Coast's peanut sauce — rich peanut paste stew with meat and eggplant, enriched with palm oil, served over rice. The West African peanut stew tradition in Ivory Coast gets extra richness from palm oil. The thick, creamy, orange-brown sauce on white rice is comfort defined.

lunch.name: Kedjenou (Slow-Cooked Chicken)
ingredients: No water added — the chicken cooks in its own juices
instructions: Place chicken pieces in a pot with all vegetables and spices
Cover tightly — NO WATER is added, the chicken releases its own moisture
Cook on very low heat for 60 min — do NOT lift the lid
The steam trapped inside cooks everything — a sealed, steaming technique
After 60 min, the chicken is incredibly tender in its own concentrated juice
The sauce is intense — pure chicken and vegetable essence, not diluted
The 'no water, no peeking' technique is the viral element
Traditionally cooked in a canari (clay pot) over charcoal
The juices at the bottom are liquid gold — concentrated flavor
Serve with attiéké or rice — the natural jus is the sauce
lunch.description: Ivory Coast's no-water chicken — sealed in a clay pot with vegetables and spices, cooking entirely in its own juices for an hour. The 'no water added, don't lift the lid' technique creates impossibly concentrated, tender chicken. Kedjenou's sealed-pot technique and the intensely flavored natural jus are viral.

lunch.name: Foutou Banane avec Sauce Graine (Pounded Plantain with Palm Nut Sauce)
ingredients: Palm nut sauce: palm fruit (boiled and pressed), fish or meat, tomato, onion, pepper, crab (optional)
instructions: Boil green plantain and cassava until very soft
Pound together in a mortar — vigorously, for 15-20 min until smooth and stretchy
The foutou should be smooth, elastic, and form a ball
Make palm nut sauce: boil palm fruits, extract the thick orange-red cream
Cook the palm cream with fish/meat, tomato, onion, pepper, crab
Simmer until thick and oily — the palm oil rises to the surface
The sauce is deep orange, rich, and intensely flavored
Serve the foutou ball with the palm nut sauce
Pinch foutou with fingers, dip in sauce — eat with hands
The pounding is the labor of love — and the shared family rhythm
lunch.description: Ivory Coast's pounded plantain and cassava served with palm nut sauce — a thick, orange, deeply flavored sauce from pressed palm fruits. The rhythmic pounding and the palm-nut-sauce richness represent Ivorian cuisine at its most traditional. The pounding technique and the sauce's intensity are the hooks.

dinner.name: Foutou Banane with Sauce Arachide
instructions: Boil and pound plantains and cassava into foutou
Make peanut sauce with chicken, tomatoes, onion
Serve foutou balls with peanut sauce
dinner.description: Pounded plantain-cassava dumplings with peanut sauce.

dinner.name: Poisson Braisé (Grilled Fish)
instructions: Score fish, marinate with spices
Grill over charcoal slowly
Make onion-tomato sauce
Serve with attiéké and alloco
dinner.description: Charcoal-grilled fish — Abidjan's evening street food.

dinner.name: Poisson Braisé (Grilled Fish Ivorian Style)
ingredients: Whole fish (tilapia, sea bream, or barracuda)
Marinade: onion, tomato, garlic, ginger, Scotch bonnet, Maggi
Attiéké or alloco (fried plantain) for serving
instructions: Score whole fish deeply on both sides
Make marinade: blend onion, tomato, garlic, ginger, Scotch bonnet, Maggi
Stuff and coat fish with the thick marinade paste
Grill over charcoal — the charcoal grilling is essential
Turn once — the fish should char and the marinade should caramelize
The charred, spice-crusted exterior and moist interior is the goal
Serve with attiéké and alloco (fried plantain)
Poisson braisé is Ivory Coast's night-out food — every maquis (street bar) serves it
The maquis culture is Abidjan — outdoor bars with grilled fish, music, cold beer
The whole grilled fish presented on the plate is a showpiece
dinner.description: Ivory Coast's charcoal-grilled fish — whole fish stuffed with spicy onion-tomato paste and charcoal-grilled at maquis (outdoor street bars). The maquis culture of Abidjan — grilled fish, cold beer, live music — is one of West Africa's most vibrant dining scenes and perpetually viral.

dinner.name: Sauce Aubergine (Eggplant Sauce)
instructions: Grill or boil eggplant until completely soft and collapsed
Mash the eggplant — it should be smooth
Sauté onion, garlic, tomato in palm oil
Add smoked fish or crab — the smokiness adds depth
Add mashed eggplant, Scotch bonnet
Simmer until thick and rich — 20 min
Season with Maggi
Serve over rice or foutou — the smoky eggplant sauce is rich and satisfying
The palm oil gives the sauce an orange tint over the purple-brown eggplant
dinner.description: Ivory Coast's smoky eggplant sauce — grilled eggplant mashed with smoked fish, palm oil, and chili. The smokiness from both the grilled eggplant and the smoked fish creates double-smoked depth. Served over rice or foutou as a deeply satisfying everyday sauce.

dinner.name: Tchep (Ivorian Jollof Rice)
instructions: Fry onion, garlic, ginger in oil until golden
Add tomato paste — fry until dark and oil separates
Add fish or chicken, brown in the tomato base
Add water, vegetables, bring to boil
Add rice, stir once, cover tightly
Cook on low heat until rice absorbs all liquid — 25-30 min
The rice should be tomato-red, fluffy, each grain separate
Ivory Coast enters the West African jollof rivalry with its own version
The palm oil gives an extra richness that sets it apart
Serve as a one-pot meal — complete and satisfying
dinner.description: Ivory Coast's entry in the West African rice wars — tomato-red, one-pot rice with fish or chicken and vegetables. Every West African country claims the best rice dish, and Ivory Coast's tchep holds its own with extra palm oil richness. The jollof debate is West Africa's most viral food argument.

snacks.name: Dégué
instructions: Steam millet couscous
Mix with sweetened yogurt and cream
Chill
Serve cold
snacks.description: Millet couscous in sweetened yogurt — a West African treat.

snacks.name: Alloco (Fried Plantain with Chili Sauce)
instructions: Slice ripe plantain diagonally — thick pieces
Deep fry until deep golden and caramelized — the natural sugars char beautifully
Make quick sauce: onion, tomato, chili, Maggi — fried together
Serve hot fried plantain with the spicy sauce on the side
The caramelized edges of the plantain are sweet-crispy perfection
Alloco is Ivory Coast's universal fried snack — served everywhere, all day
The sweet plantain and spicy sauce contrast is addictive
Every maquis, every street corner, every home — alloco is Ivorian life
snacks.description: Ivory Coast's fried plantain — caramelized golden and served with fiery onion-chili sauce. Alloco is the Ivorian national snack — at every maquis, school gate, and home. The sweet-caramelized-meets-spicy-sauce contrast is West African snacking perfection.

snacks.name: Dèguè (Millet Yogurt)
instructions: Steam millet couscous until cooked, let cool completely
Mix cooled millet with yogurt or fermented milk
Add condensed milk or sugar, vanilla
Add nutmeg or pineapple pieces if desired
Chill — serve cold
The tiny millet grains in creamy yogurt create a unique texture
Dèguè is Ivory Coast's dessert drink — somewhere between a smoothie and a pudding
The texture is the appeal — grainy-smooth, creamy-crunchy
Served at celebrations and as a refreshing afternoon treat
snacks.description: Ivory Coast's millet-yogurt dessert — tiny steamed millet grains folded into sweetened yogurt creating a unique grainy-creamy texture. Dèguè is somewhere between a smoothie and a pudding, served at celebrations and as a cooling afternoon refreshment.

snacks.name: Placali (Fermented Cassava Paste)
instructions: Ferment cassava for several days — the sourness develops
Grind fermented cassava, mix with water
Cook the paste, stirring vigorously — it thickens dramatically
Continue stirring until smooth, stretchy, and translucent
The placali should be elastic and slightly sour
Shape into a smooth ball
Serve with any sauce — peanut, palm nut, leaf sauce
Tear pieces of placali and dip into sauce — eat with hands
The stretchy, slightly sour texture is unique to fermented cassava
Placali is Ivory Coast's second staple after attiéké — both from cassava
snacks.description: Ivory Coast's fermented cassava paste — stretchy, slightly sour, translucent, and eaten by tearing pieces and dipping in rich sauces. Placali shows cassava's incredible versatility — the same root becomes attiéké (couscous), placali (paste), and foutou (pounded). Ivory Coast is the world capital of cassava cuisine.

desserts.name: Claclo (Plantain Fritters)
instructions: Mash plantains, mix with flour, sugar, vanilla
Fry spoonfuls until golden
desserts.description: Sweet plantain fritters — dessert or snack.

desserts.name: Beignets de Maïs (Corn Fritters)
ingredients: Fresh corn (grated from cob) or cornmeal
instructions: Grate fresh corn from cobs (or use cornmeal mixed with water)
Mix with sugar, flour, egg, nutmeg
The batter should be thick and scoopable
Drop spoonfuls into hot oil
Fry until golden — 3-4 min
The corn gives a natural sweetness and a subtle corn flavor
Drain briefly, dust with sugar if desired
These are Ivory Coast's afternoon sweet snack — with coffee or on their own
The fresh corn version has texture — little corn bits in the crispy exterior
desserts.description: Ivorian corn fritters — fresh corn grated and fried into golden, naturally sweet puffs. The corn gives both sweetness and texture. Afternoon snack tradition across Ivory Coast, served with coffee at the maquis.

desserts.name: Claclo (Banana Fritters with Coconut)
instructions: Mash ripe bananas until smooth
Mix with flour, sugar, grated coconut, nutmeg
The batter should be thick and scoopable
Drop spoonfuls into hot oil
Fry until golden brown — 3-4 min
The coconut gives extra crunch and tropical flavor to the banana fritters
Drain briefly, dust with sugar if desired
Claclo is Ivory Coast's banana-coconut fritter — a twist on basic banana fritters
The coconut addition is the Ivorian signature — more textured than plain banana beignets
desserts.description: Ivory Coast's banana-coconut fritters — ripe banana batter studded with grated coconut and fried golden. The coconut adds crunch and tropical depth that plain banana fritters lack. Claclo is the Ivorian afternoon treat at every maquis and street corner.

drinks.name: Bangui (Palm Wine)
instructions: Tap palm tree at dawn
Collect sap in calabash
Drink fresh — ferments quickly
drinks.description: Fresh palm wine, best drunk the morning it's tapped.

drinks.name: Gnamakoudji (Ginger Juice)
instructions: Grate ginger, squeeze out juice
Mix with water, sugar, lemon
Chill, serve with mint
drinks.description: Potent ginger juice — refreshing and spicy.

drinks.name: Bissap (Hibiscus Drink)
instructions: Boil hibiscus in water 10-15 min — the liquid turns deep ruby red
Strain, add sugar generously
Add mint, vanilla, or pineapple juice
Chill — serve ice cold over ice
Bissap is West Africa's universal hibiscus drink — Ivory Coast makes it strong and sweet
The deep red color is photogenic and striking
Rich in vitamin C — it's both delicious and healthy
Essential during Ramadan and at every celebration
drinks.description: Ivory Coast's bissap — hibiscus flowers steeped into a deep ruby-red, sweet, tart drink served ice cold. The universal West African refreshment, essential at celebrations and during Ramadan. The jewel-red color and the tart-sweet profile are endlessly photogenic.

drinks.name: Bangui (Palm Wine)
ingredients: Palm tree sap (tapped from oil palm or raffia palm)
instructions: A tapper climbs the palm tree and cuts into the crown
Sap collects in a calabash or bottle — sweet and milky when fresh
Within hours, wild yeasts ferment it into mildly alcoholic palm wine
Fresh bangui (sweet toddy) is best in the first 24 hours
By day 2-3, it becomes stronger and more sour — bandji
The fermentation window for 'perfect' bangui is narrow
Palm wine culture is central to Ivorian social life — shared at gatherings
The tapper's skill (climbing tall palm trees) is respected and dangerous
Bangui is served at naming ceremonies, weddings, and funerals
In Ivory Coast, palm wine is not just a drink — it's a cultural bond
drinks.description: Ivory Coast's palm wine — sap tapped from palm trees and naturally fermented by wild yeasts. Bangui is central to Ivorian social life — served at every ceremony from birth to death. The tree-climbing tapper, the narrow fermentation window, and the cultural significance make palm wine one of Africa's most storied drinks.
